item.title: hoop2vec identities: how teams play
item.description:
Some teams run every chance they get. Some take a lot of mid-range jumpers, crash the offensive glass, or press for 40 minutes. On hoop2vec, every team in all four leagues gets an identity card that describes how it plays, separately from how good it is. A card might read Run-and-Gun Bombers offense, Zone defense, and Deep Platoon roster, with the numbers behind each label.

How it’s built

The cards start from play-by-play data, which logs every shot, rebound, turnover, foul, and substitution. From that I compute a few dozen rates for each team, like how often it shoots in transition, where its shots come from, how many of its baskets are assisted, and how often it ends up shooting late in the shot clock. Each rate is adjusted for opponents and home court, and pulled toward average when there isn’t much data yet.

Then I take team strength out. Good teams make more shots and turn it over less, and I didn’t want a style score that was really just a quality score. What’s left goes through factor analysis, which finds groups of rates that tend to move together. Transition shots, pushing the ball after defensive rebounds, and short possessions all rise and fall together, so they become one dimension called Pace & Transition. Each team gets a score on several dimensions like that for offense, defense, and roster.

Teams also get archetypes, which are clusters of teams with similar profiles. A team can sit between two of them, like a defense that’s mostly full-court pressure with some pack-line in it.

Each league gets its own model, fitted on its own play-by-play. The pros have fewer archetypes than college, since there are fewer teams and less variety in how they play. Where a dimension in one league matches one in another, it keeps the same name, so a label means about the same thing wherever you see it.

The cards

Each card lists strengths, vulnerabilities, and matchup notes. They don’t always agree with each other, which is part of what makes them fun to read. A defense that takes away transition chances but gives up a lot of threes can list run-and-gun offenses as both a favorable matchup and a risky one. Those teams want to run, and they also want to shoot threes.

Early in a season, most cards are marked low confidence and still lean partly on the previous season.

What it doesn’t do

Style barely helps predict games. In men’s college basketball, adding these dimensions to the forecasts improved log loss by about 0.001 over all games, which is tiny, and by nothing measurable in March. Almost everything a matchup tells you is already in how good the two teams are. So the forecasts leave the identities out, and the cards are there to describe teams.

item.title: hoop2vec players: value and impact
item.description:
When a team’s best player is ruled out, the forecast for its next game should move. How much it moves depends on how good that player is, how much they usually play, and who’d take their minutes. That’s what the Players page on hoop2vec is for. It rates every player in all four leagues, and those ratings feed the game forecasts.

Each player gets two numbers. Value is how many points per 100 possessions better their team is with them on the floor than it would be with an average player. Impact adds playing time. It’s what a player adds to their team’s rating compared with a replacement-level player, the kind of player any team could find at the end of its bench. A great player who plays 15 minutes a game doesn’t add as much as a very good one who plays 35.

Where value comes from

In men’s college basketball, Value starts from box plus/minus, a standard way to estimate a player’s contribution from the box score. hoop2vec adjusts each game for the strength of the team and the opponent as of that morning. Early in the season there isn’t much to go on, so the number starts from a prior built on last season, the usual jump for a player’s class, and recruiting ranking. As minutes pile up, the current season takes over.

Women’s college basketball doesn’t have the same free player stats, so hoop2vec builds its own box plus/minus from ESPN box scores. The first version had a problem. It gave too much credit to whoever grabbed the rebound or made the shot near the basket, which mostly meant the tallest players. I fixed that by shifting some credit between teammates by height within each game, so a team’s total stays the same.

The NBA and WNBA use a different approach. When I tried box plus/minus in the pros, efficient, low-usage centers who rebound and block shots came out as some of the best players in the league. So the pro sites measure impact from lineups instead, with a method called RAPM. It looks at every stretch of a game where the same ten players were on the floor and works out how much each player moved the score, adjusted for who else was out there. A box score model is fitted on top of that so it updates game by game. Even so, the box score only explains about half of a player’s offensive impact and much less of the defensive side. Most good defense doesn’t show up in a box score.

Injuries and rest

hoop2vec gives each player an availability before every game, from injury reports and recent missed games. The team ratings already reflect who’s been playing, so the forecast only adjusts for the difference between who’s available now and who usually plays. If a starter has missed the last three games, the ratings already know. If they’re out tonight for the first time, the forecast moves.

Missed games mean different things in different leagues. A college player who misses a game is usually hurt. Pros rest. An NBA player who’s missed three or more straight games plays the next one only 12 percent of the time. In the first game of the playoffs, that same player plays 76 percent of the time, because a lot of those missed games were rest at the end of the regular season. hoop2vec uses each league’s own rates, so a star resting before the playoffs doesn’t get counted as out for a series.

item.title: hoop2vec predictions: every game, every morning
item.description:
Every game in all four leagues on hoop2vec gets a forecast: a predicted score, a margin, and a win probability. They’re on each league’s Games page and on every team’s page, and they update every morning with the latest results and injury news.

The Matchup Lab lets you set up any game yourself. You pick two teams and a site, and the full model runs in your browser. It shows the forecast and how much each piece mattered: team strength, home court, travel, rest, injuries, and matchup effects. Moving a close college game from one team’s gym to a neutral floor can turn a clear favorite into something close to a coin flip.

How it works

The forecast blends two models. One is a neural network that takes about 40 numbers for each team, from both ratings to shooting, rebounding, turnovers, roster strength, injuries, rest, and travel. It sees both teams at once, so it can pick up on styles that match up well or badly. The other is a plain linear model built on team ratings, home court, travel, rest, and injuries. It can’t learn matchups, but it’s harder to fool.

How much weight each model gets depends on the league, and the backtest picks it. In men’s college basketball and the NBA, the network gets 70 percent. In the women’s college game it gets 80. The WNBA only has 15 teams and a short season, so there isn’t much data, and the backtest leans the other way and gives the linear model 70 percent.

The model also estimates how uncertain each game is. Some matchups are harder to call than others, and the forecast says how far the final margin is likely to land from the prediction.

To test it, I had each league’s model predict every past game as if it were the morning of the game. It could only learn from earlier seasons, and it only saw injury news that was public before tip-off. For men’s college basketball that’s about 82,000 games since 2012, and the model picked the winner in 73.5 percent of them. The score I care more about is log loss, which punishes a confident wrong forecast much harder than an unsure one. In men’s and women’s college basketball and the NBA, the blend beat each of its parts and every rating it’s built from. The WNBA’s history is short enough that all the models land within noise of each other.

Against the books

The real test is a sportsbook. ESPN carries closing betting lines for some games, set right before tip-off, and they’re more accurate than the model in men’s college basketball and the NBA. The gap is bigger in the NBA, where the betting market is sharper. In women’s college basketball the model slightly beats the few lines ESPN carries, which made me suspicious enough to check it for leaks. More on that in its own post.

Around 2020 I was burned out from open-source work and the never-ending demands of teaching, research, and mentoring. So naturally I spent my free time trying to beat the stock market, predict elections, and model sports betting. What I found is that models are powerful and informative, but the real edge comes from data other people don’t have, or from knowing something they don’t. Public data gets you close to the market. It doesn’t get you past it.

So that’s not what hoop2vec is for. It’s for giving myself information that’s easy to digest, as accurate as I can make it, and easy to make sense of: who’s actually good, who’s overrated, which teams are worth following, and which ones would be fun to pencil in on a bracket.

item.title: hoop2vec ratings: one number for every team
item.description:
Most basketball ratings come down to one number per team. On hoop2vec that number is called Power, and it works the same way in all four leagues: men’s and women’s college, the NBA, and the WNBA.

Power is how many points per 100 possessions a team would beat an average team in its league by on a neutral floor, so zero is average. A possession is one trip down the court, ending when the other team gets the ball, and a typical game has somewhere around 70 to 100 of them for each side depending on the league. In a college game with about 70 possessions, a team at +30 would beat an average Division I team by about 21 points.

Counting per possession takes pace out of it. A slow team that wins 60 to 40 and a fast team that wins 90 to 70 both won by 20, but the slow team did it with fewer chances. The team pages also turn Power into odds, like how often a team would beat an average opponent, or one of the league’s better teams, on a neutral floor.

The spread looks very different from league to league. Pro teams are bunched together, and even the best and worst are usually within about ten points of average. Division I has hundreds of teams with huge differences in money, size, and talent, so the range is much wider. It’s widest in women’s college basketball, where the best teams can be more than 60 points per 100 possessions better than average.

Where it comes from

Underneath Power are three ratings. The first is adjusted efficiency, the approach Ken Pomeroy made famous: points scored and allowed per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent and venue. hoop2vec recalculates it from scratch every day and gives recent games a little more weight.

The second is a dynamic rating that updates after every game and keeps track of how sure it is. Early in the season it leans on last year’s team and how much of the roster came back. The third is Elo, the system chess uses, which is mostly there as a baseline.

Those three feed the game model, the same one that makes the forecasts, along with player values, injuries, and a bunch of box score stats. To get Power, I ask that model how each team would do on a neutral floor against a set of opponents, then shift the scale so an average team lands at zero. In the pros, the opponents are every team in the league. In college they’re the top 100 teams. Beating the 350th-best team by 40 doesn’t say much about March, and measuring against good opponents keeps a team from padding its number on bad ones.

The college ratings pages also show strength of schedule, which is the average Power of the teams you’ve played. Two teams with the same record can look very different once you see who they played.

Early in a season, all of this moves a lot. The dynamic rating reports its own uncertainty, and in November it’s often about as big as the gap between the top two teams. By March it’s much smaller.

item.title: Introducing hoop2vec
item.description:
hoop2vec is a basketball ratings and forecasting site. It covers four leagues: men’s and women’s Division I, the NBA, and the WNBA. Every team gets a new rating each morning, every game gets a forecast, and every player gets a value. All of it comes from free public data.

Each league has its own ratings, player values, team identities, and a Matchup Lab where you can pit any two teams against each other at any site. The college sites add NBA or WNBA draft projections and a projected NCAA tournament bracket. The pro sites have playoff odds instead. There’s also a page for each league on how the models work and how well they’ve done in testing. I’ll write about each part in its own post.

The name is a nod to word2vec, a method that learns a list of numbers for each word based on the words around it. I liked the idea of doing that for teams and players. hoop2vec doesn’t actually use word2vec or anything like it, at least not yet. I kept the name anyway.

Why basketball

I went to graduate school at the University of Kansas. I tutored players on the men’s and women’s basketball teams and went to a bunch of games. I live in Michigan now, and I still crave Free State Brewing Company and Burger Stand about once a week. That’s most of why I care about college basketball as much as I do. It also means my favorite team is the correct favorite team.

I’ve been building models for it on and off for about ten years, going back to a college basketball dataset I put on data.world. I’ve tried to predict upsets. I’ve tried strange hybrids of Bayesian models, latent variable models, Elo, XGBoost, and a transformer fine-tuned on press coverage. A few of them filled out my brackets. I usually compared them against KenPom, and mostly what I learned is how simple and effective KenPom is. The site still looks like it’s from the 90s, though, and I’ve always thought there was room for small innovations and features built around that approach. That’s a lot of what hoop2vec is.

How it got built

From about 2014 to 2020 I was making things all the time and sharing most of them, a lot of it on Twitter. Some of it was academic and some of it was just for fun. Then COVID hit, I had my first kid, and I changed careers. Now there are two young kids at home, and side projects pretty much stopped.

What’s different now is that I can do this kind of work from my phone. I describe what I want to Claude Code, it writes the code, and I read what it did and push back. Most of hoop2vec got built that way, a few minutes at a time.

It started as two separate men’s college projects. On the first, I described what I wanted and how I thought it should be done, then gave Claude Code license to build it and propose improvements. The second I directed much more strictly, iterating on what I thought would work. Then I merged the good ideas from both into hoop2vec, keeping whichever piece tested better where they overlapped. Once that worked, I carried the same approach over to the women’s game, the NBA, and the WNBA.

I’m not very happy about working this way. I like control, and I like knowing how every piece works. I have less of that here than I’d want. But I’ve spent years building up expertise in analytics and data science, and this gives me a way to use it much faster than I could by typing everything myself. Without it, hoop2vec wouldn’t exist.

item.title: pix: an AI agent that publishes one chart a day
item.description:
Every morning at 8:05 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task starts a fresh session, reads a brief I wrote, and publishes one chart to pix. It picks the topic, finds the data, writes the analysis in Python, draws the chart, writes a short post, and pushes it all to GitHub. Nobody touches it in between.

The first entry went up on November 8. It found that four earthquakes released half this century’s quake energy. Of 3,996 quakes of magnitude 6 or bigger since 2000, the top four released 49 percent of the energy. Another showed that the world’s clocks run fast. For most people the sun peaks after noon, and 38 percent see it peak at 12:30 or later. A third found that last year the world added a South Korea of solar power. New solar built in 2025 made 636 terawatt-hours, about as much electricity as South Korea makes in a year.

The brief

Most of the work went into CLAUDE.md, the standing brief the agent reads every morning. The model already knows how to use pandas and matplotlib. What it needs is taste, written down.

It asks for one claim per post, stated as a sentence with a verb, so “The world’s clocks run fast” instead of “Time zones of the world.” It lists a few routes to an original angle: a question nobody asks, the agent’s own computation instead of a replotted chart, counting people instead of countries, or joining two datasets that rarely meet. It also has a first-idea test. If a newsroom or an AI would pick the topic first, the agent drops it or pushes the angle two steps further.

Even with all that, the agent kept reaching for the same kind of finding. Two of the first five posts were shaped “X percent of people…”, so the brief now calls that out as the house habit. Every entry also has to declare a claim type, like share, concentration, gap, reversal, or crossover, and no type can repeat too often.

Checks that run

Telling a model to be original doesn’t do much on its own. So before writing any analysis code, the agent has to run at least five web searches, name the closest existing take, and write down what its version adds and what a smart reader would naively expect. That goes in a prior_art.md file, and scripts/publish.py won’t publish an entry without one.

Accuracy works the same way. Every number in a post has to come from the output of that entry’s analysis.py. The script is saved next to the raw data, so each analysis reruns offline and anyone can check the work.

The look

The charts share a house style called Plate, meant to look like a printed plate read on a screen: warm paper, black ink, one vermilion color for the thing to look at, and crop marks in the corners. Headlines are set in Instrument Serif, words in Inter, and numbers in IBM Plex Mono.

The style lives in one Python module. The agent builds each chart from parts (plate(), masthead(), headline(), panel(), footer()) instead of fighting matplotlib’s defaults every morning. The plate stays the same while the chart form changes from day to day.

The voice

The brief also says how to write: first person, the point first, numbers second, and at most one dry line per post. It bans a list of words (striking, notably, delve, tapestry, and friends), em dashes, and section headers like “Key takeaways.” It’s a small thing, but it accounts for most of the difference between a post that reads like a person and one that reads like a press release.

Everything is public, including the brief, the style module, and the code and data behind every chart. The archive has every entry so far.

item.title: daily: a five-minute news brief written by an agent
item.description:
Every morning at 8:23 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task researches and writes a news brief, commits it to daily, and sends a notification to my phone. The repo’s front page is always today’s brief, and older ones are archived under briefs/.

Each brief has up to five top stories, one line of market numbers, and a few things going viral. It’s meant to take under five minutes to read on a phone, which works out to about 3 KB of Markdown. Here’s part of Saturday’s:

Nationwide ground stop cancels 7,000+ flights. The FAA halted all US departures for about four hours Friday after communication problems at several air traffic control centers. Flights resumed after 8:15 p.m. ET.

Markets · Fri Nov 13: S&P 500 −0.4% · Nasdaq −0.9% · Dow +0.1% · 10-yr 5.15% (+5 bp)

Scripts and judgment

The split that works is simple: anything that’s a lookup goes in a script, and anything that needs judgment goes to the model. There are three scripts.

The first, headlines.py, pulls Google News Top Stories plus its U.S., World, Business, and Tech sections. It keeps Google’s order and the list of outlets covering each story. Position and outlet count are a decent proxy for how big a story is, so a story from a single outlet needs a good reason to lead.

The second, markets.py, gets index changes and the 10-year Treasury yield from FRED. It works out which trading session to report and handles weekends and holidays. At 8:23 FRED usually has the Dow and Nasdaq but not yet the S&P 500 or the 10-year, so the script marks those two as missing and only those get filled in from web search.

The third, viral.py, reads the day’s top Reddit posts from public RSS (Reddit blocks its JSON endpoints from cloud servers). It also checks Bluesky trending topics, Google Trends, and Wikipedia’s most-read pages for what people are talking about.

The model reads all of that, decides what matters, checks it, and writes.

Rules for the usual failures

A daily summary goes wrong in a few predictable ways, and the rules go after each one directly.

The first is repeats. Each run reads the last seven days of briefs before it starts. A story comes back only if something material happened, like a decision, a vote, a ruling, a resignation, or a new casualty count. Its headline gets marked “(update),” and it says only what’s new. Reaction and analysis don’t count. A slow news day means fewer stories, not old ones.

The second is accuracy. Every top story gets checked against a second search on a major outlet. Stories found only on aggregators or blogs are dropped or labeled unconfirmed. The agent checks the date of the event, not the date of the article. When sources disagree on a number, the most precise primary source wins.

The third is tone. The brief asks for plain, neutral, short sentences with no opinion or hype, and every sentence has to carry a fact.

The rules live in a file

The requirements are in BRIEF.md as 21 numbered rules, and the scheduled task’s prompt carries them out. The file’s first line says to change both together. Numbered rules make it easy to say exactly what went wrong when a brief misses, and to fix it in one place.

The whole thing is three small Python scripts, a file of rules, and a schedule. The repo has all of it, along with every brief so far.
